glossary.Straining: Pushing hard to pass a stool.
glossary.Incomplete evacuation: The feeling that the bowel has not emptied fully after opening.
glossary.Immobility: Being unable to move around much, which slows the gut.
glossary.Functional bowel disorders: Gut symptoms with no structural cause, such as irritable bowel syndrome.
glossary.Iron tablets: Oral iron supplements, a common cause of constipation and dark stools.
glossary.Intestinal motility: Movement of the gut wall that pushes contents along.
glossary.Secondary causes: Constipation caused by another disease rather than lifestyle.
glossary.Endocrine: Relating to hormones and the glands that make them.
glossary.Parkinson's: Neurodegenerative disease that slows movement and also slows gut transit.
glossary.Spinal cord disease: Damage to the spinal cord that disrupts bowel nerve control.
glossary.Palpable: Able to be felt on examination.
glossary.Rectal mass: A lump felt in the rectum on DRE, which may be cancer.
glossary.Type 7: Entirely liquid stool on the Bristol stool chart.
glossary.Neonate: A baby in the first 28 days of life.
glossary.Full-term: Born at 37 weeks of pregnancy or later.
glossary.Innervation: The nerve supply to a part of the body.
glossary.Structural lesion: A physical abnormality such as a tumour or stricture.
glossary.Rectal biopsy: A small sample of rectal wall taken to look at under the microscope.
glossary.Clinical diagnosis: A diagnosis made from history and examination alone.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count, which can show anaemia.
glossary.Calcium: Blood calcium level, checked because hypercalcaemia causes constipation.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood tests of kidney function and hydration.
glossary.Red flags: Features such as weight loss or rectal bleeding that suggest serious disease.
glossary.Colonoscopy: Camera test looking inside the whole colon.
glossary.Microcytic anaemia: Anaemia with small red cells, usually from iron deficiency.
glossary.Laxative: A drug that helps the bowels open.
glossary.Digital stimulation: Using a gloved finger in the rectum to trigger bowel emptying.
glossary.Stool softener: A laxative that lets water into stool to soften it, such as docusate.
glossary.Opioid-induced constipation: Constipation caused by opioid painkillers acting on gut receptors.
glossary.Bowel obstruction: Blockage of the bowel causing vomiting, distension, pain and no flatus.
glossary.Distension: Swelling of the abdomen from gas or fluid.
glossary.Colonic transit: The movement of stool through the colon.
glossary.Defecatory mechanism: The coordinated muscle actions needed to pass stool.
glossary.Parasympathetic: The rest-and-digest nervous system, which drives gut movement via acetylcholine.
glossary.Smooth muscle: Involuntary muscle in the gut wall.
glossary.Peristalsis: Waves of muscle contraction that push contents along the gut.
glossary.Neural crest cell: Embryonic cells that migrate to form nerves, including the gut's nerve network.
glossary.Embryogenesis: Development of the embryo in early pregnancy.
glossary.Functional obstruction: Blockage caused by bowel that cannot relax, without a physical blockage.
glossary.Faecal mass: The bulk of stool in the bowel.
glossary.Bowel lumen: The hollow inside of the bowel.
glossary.Haemorrhoids: Swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal that can bleed painlessly.
glossary.Muscarinic: Acetylcholine receptors in the gut that anticholinergic drugs block.
